input: Feedback control is a cornerstone of process operations, and a temperature loop on a process vessel offers a particularly instructive illustration of the underlying principles in action. The role of the temperature loop is to hold the temperature of the vessel at its desired set point by acting on a heating or cooling stream. The first element in the loop is the sensor, which measures the temperature of the vessel contents and transmits the measured value to the controller. The sensor is typically installed directly in the contents or in a well in the vessel wall, and it is important to appreciate that the loop acts on the reading rather than on the true temperature itself; consequently, a sensor that lags behind the contents, or that reads a wall temperature instead of the bulk, quietly introduces its error into every action the loop subsequently takes. The controller then compares the measured value against the set point and calculates the required correction from the difference between them, known as the error. Its output is passed to the final element, namely a control valve on the heating or cooling line, which adjusts its position in order to change the heat input in the direction the controller demands. Crucially, the sign of the feedback is negative: a rise in temperature above the set point reduces the heating or increases the cooling, whereas a fall below the set point produces the reverse response, so that the correction always opposes the deviation that gave rise to it. It is precisely this negative character that makes the loop stable in structure, since each departure from the set point generates an action that works to reduce that departure. The description given here concerns structure only; how far the valve travels for a given error, and how rapidly the loop responds, are matters of tuning, and no tuning values are stated.

The sensor measures the temperature of the vessel contents and sends the measured value to the controller. The sensor sits in the contents or in a well in the vessel wall, and the reading, not the true temperature, is what the loop acts on; a sensor that lags behind the contents, or reads a wall temperature rather than the bulk, carries its error into every action the loop takes. The controller compares the measured value with the set point and calculates the correction from the difference between them, the error. The controller output goes to the final element, a control valve on the heating or cooling line, which moves to change the heat input in the direction the controller demands. The sign of the feedback is negative. A rise in temperature above the set point reduces the heating or increases the cooling, and a fall in temperature below the set point does the reverse, so the correction opposes the deviation that produced it. Negative feedback is what makes the loop stable in structure: each departure from the set point generates an action that reduces the departure. The vessel contents are the load on the loop: heat drawn off by the process, or added by it, appears first as a change in the measured temperature, and the loop answers that change through the one stream it controls.
